text:
The countdown ticked like a bomb in the silence of the control room. Three minutes. The window was closing, not with a slam, but with a whisper of atmospheric pressure shifting against the hull.

“Abort,” Commander Elara Vance said, her voice steady as bedrock through the comms loop. “The primary seal is weeping.”

“Weeping?” Ground Control’s David Halloway snapped, his knuckles white around his headset. “Telemetry shows nominal variance. You’re hallucinating from pre-launch adrenaline. We launch or we wait eighteen months for the next alignment. Do you understand the cost?”

“I understand physics, David. Physics doesn’t negotiate with schedules.”

“Physics doesn’t have to fund this program! The optics are perfect *now*. Move your hand off the abort switch.”

Elara watched the fuel gauge tremble. She could feel the cold sweat trickling down her spine, a phantom touch in the vacuum-sealed suit. The red button under her thumb was warm, alive with potential failure. Or success.

“It’s not a glitch,” she whispered.

“It’s fear,” he shouted, breaking protocol. “And fear is expensive. Push forward.”

Two minutes. The hum of the engines rose to a scream. Elara looked at the telemetry screen, then at the button. She didn’t press it. Not yet. But she didn’t pull her hand away either.
